Patrobas
PAT-roh-bas
proper noun
From the Greek Patrobas, a shortened form meaning “life of his father” or “paternal,” likely a contraction of Patrobios.

Biblical Definition

Patrobas is one of the believers at Rome whom the apostle Paul singles out for greeting in the closing chapter of his great epistle, named in a cluster of five: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Rom 16:14). Of his life, his trade, his trials, and his death the Word tells us nothing further; he is a name and no more. Yet that very obscurity preaches. The Holy Spirit, who omitted whole reigns of kings in a sentence, took care to set down Patrobas by name in the imperishable record of Scripture. He was known and loved by Paul, and known and chosen of God before the foundation of the world. The grouping “and the brethren which are with them” suggests Patrobas belonged to a household or house-fellowship of saints, the ordinary soil in which the early church grew. Tradition counts him among the seventy and makes him a martyr, but Scripture is silent, and where Scripture is silent we hold our peace. What we may say with certainty is that his name is written in heaven (Luk 10:20), which is honor enough. The roll of Romans 16 is a standing rebuke to every notion that only the prominent matter to God; the Head of the church numbers His least members and forgets none of them.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Christian at Rome greeted by Paul in Romans 16, of whom nothing else is recorded in Scripture.

expand to see more

PATROBAS, a believer in the church at Rome to whom the apostle Paul sent salutation.

Named in a group of five with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, and Hermes (Rom 16:14).

His name is Greek, a contracted form meaning “life of his father.”

Listed with “the brethren which are with them,” marking a household of saints.

Later tradition reckons him among the seventy and a martyr, though Scripture is silent.

Key Scripture

Rom 16:14 — "Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them."

Luk 10:20 — "Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven."

Rom 16:16 — "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you."

Phi 4:3 — "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life."

Modern Corruption

The honour of the obscure saint, remembered by name in heaven though forgotten on earth.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Patrobas is the dignity God assigns to His unknown people. A single name in a list of greetings, he stands for the thousands of faithful who never preach, never write, never lead, and yet are precious to Christ and inscribed in the Lamb’s book of life.

Our age measures worth by visibility and platform; the Spirit measures it by union with Christ. Patrobas rebukes the hunger for recognition that gnaws even at believers. To be known by God is infinitely more than to be known by men, and the saint who labours in obscurity loses nothing, for the Judge of all the earth keeps a perfect record and will not forget the work and labour of love shown toward His name.

Hebrew Roots

A Greek personal name compounded from pater (father) and a life-element, common among Roman freedmen.

expand to see more

Patrobas — a contracted Greek name, likely from Patrobios, “life of his father.”

The element pater, “father,” underlies the Latin pater and English paternal.

Shortened personal names of this form were common among slaves and freedmen in imperial Rome.

Its appearance fits the mixed company of the Roman church, Jew and Gentile, bond and free.

The name survives solely because the Spirit recorded it in Romans 16.

Usage

"Paul did not overlook the least of the saints, but greeted Patrobas by name."

"Like Patrobas, many believers serve faithfully and are remembered only in heaven."

"The mention of Patrobas reminds us that no member of Christ’s body is forgotten."
